**Bank Time**

The clock on the bank in Orrin ran seven minutes fast for forty-one years, and I can tell you how a town absorbs a thing like that.

First it's a complaint. My grandfather remembered that phase: letters to the paper, people standing outside the pharmacy before it opened, checking their watches and scowling up at the square. Then it's a joke. Then it's arithmetic, done so automatically that nobody experiences it as arithmetic. You looked up, saw 8:52, and knew 8:45, the way you read a word without sounding out the letters.

By the time I was a child, there was vocabulary. There was bank time and there was true time. My mother would say dinner was at six bank, meaning be home by 5:53, and I never once thought this strange. The school ran true. The buses ran true. The Methodists ran bank, for reasons no one could explain, and the Catholics ran true, and a few mixed marriages had their own arrangements.

You could spot a stranger by watching them cross the square. They'd glance up and quicken. Locals glanced up and slowed down.

That's the part I think about most. Several times a day, the clock did the same thing to each of us. You looked up, your stomach dropped because you were late, and then you remembered, and seven minutes were handed back to you. It was a small mercy, repeated for four decades. I believe it made us a slightly calmer town than we would otherwise have been, though I can't prove it and wouldn't know how to try.

Nobody fixed it because fixing it was nobody's job. The bank changed owners four times. The clock belonged to the building, and the building belonged to a holding company in another state. The mechanism could be reached only by a ladder inside a locked closet, and the key had left town in the pocket of a manager who retired to Arizona in 1983. Each obstacle was small, but together they made the clock as permanent as weather.

Then in 2015 the branch got a new manager named Carys Bell, who was from elsewhere and was competent. She found a locksmith within the week. She had the clock corrected on a Tuesday morning without announcing it, on the reasonable assumption that no one could object to a clock being right.

For about a year afterward, the whole town was late.

Everyone knew it had been fixed. It was on the front page, above the fold, with a photograph of the repairman on his ladder. But knowing didn't reach the place where the subtraction lived. People looked up, took off seven, and strolled. My mother missed the opening of every meeting she attended that year. The pharmacy's morning rush moved. The Methodists had a real crisis, because bank time had become true time. Their service now began seven minutes earlier than their bodies understood it to. For a while they started at 10:03, which pleased no one.

People were angry at Carys Bell in a way they couldn't justify, so it came out sideways. They complained about the new fee schedule and the parking. She had corrected an error, and nobody could stand up at a council meeting and say they wanted the error back. But she had also taken away something that only we knew. The clock had been a quiet test of belonging, and now it said the same thing to everybody.

Someone did eventually stand up at a council meeting. Walt Greer proposed that the town formally request the clock be set seven minutes fast, "as a matter of heritage." It went to a vote and lost three to two, which was closer than anyone expected. The council had no authority over a private clock anyway. Carys Bell was in the room. She said afterward that she'd have done it if they'd asked. I believe her. She still runs the branch. She told me once that for the first two years, customers would look at the clock, then at her, then at the clock again.

The subtraction faded, mostly. Children born since then have never heard of bank time, and when the older ones say it, they hear a figure of speech. The Methodists start at ten. The square has a clock on it that tells you what time it is.

My mother never stopped, though. I was home last spring, walking her to an appointment we were already cutting close. Halfway across the square she glanced up, and I watched her lips move very slightly, the way they have my whole life.

"We've got time," she said.

We didn't. I slowed down anyway.

I'm weighing a few other directions: a tide pool piece, a note on the person who names paint colors, or a lexicon's final entries. Each feels too familiar, so I'm settling on a short story about a town whose clock runs seven minutes fast and where everyone has quietly adjusted to it.

I'm weighing how the clock's error could become something the town shares: the fix would erase the test of who belongs there. I'm imagining a narrator who grew up in Orrin and came back, for whom those seven minutes are a small daily gift. Then a well-meaning repair leaves everyone still subtracting seven and running late, and I'm wondering whether anyone ever climbs up to set it forward again.

I'm settling into the plainest form for the piece: a short prose draft, first person, aiming for well under the thousand-word limit, with the clock's history as the opening image.

I'm picturing how strangers and locals move through the square differently: visitors glance up and hurry, while locals glance up and ease off, because the clock hands each of them seven minutes back. I think that small repeated relief may have made the town a little calmer than it otherwise would have been, though I can't prove it. The next thing I'm turning over is why nobody ever got around to fixing it.

I'm picturing the story's turn now: a new branch manager, Carys Bell, who finds the key within a week and quietly corrects the clock on an ordinary Tuesday, assuming no one could object to a clock being right. The next year the town is late, because everyone still subtracts seven, and the narrator's mother keeps missing the first seven minutes of everything, even though the fix is on the front page.

Now I'm weighing how the town's split over the clock would play out: the Methodists settling on 10:03 for a while, pleasing nobody, and the anger at Carys Bell coming out sideways because she removed something only the town knew. I'm also picturing the council vote failing, the subtraction slowly fading for everyone but my mother, who still glances up and takes off seven minutes as she crosses the square.

I'm settling the ending: my mother saying "we've got time" as we cross the square, and me slowing down with her anyway. I also want to note that Carys Bell stayed on and is still the one people ask about the clock, so I'll keep that part brief.
